source: KDT8 ch1; RangDale9 ch1-3; Katzung16 ch1; GG14 ch1

cards.front: What was materia medica, and why could it not become a true science of drug action?
cards.back: Materia medica was the older study of preparing drugs and their medical uses, the forerunner of pharmacology. Real understanding of mechanism was blocked because there were no methods to purify active agents from crude materials and no experimental way to test ideas about how drugs act; therapeutics was governed by authority and dogma rather than experiment.

cards.front: Who first purified morphine from opium, when, and why was this important?
cards.back: Friedrich Serturner, a young German apothecary, in 1805. It showed that a defined chemical, not a vital force, produced the effect of a plant extract, and it opened the era of purifying active plant principles (quinine, digitalis, atropine, ephedrine, strychnine and others).

cards.front: Give four examples of drugs whose use began from human experience with plants.
cards.back: Caffeine (coffee berries, noticed from the behaviour of goats); atropine (Atropa belladonna extract used to dilate the pupils); ephedrine (Chinese herb ma huang, used as a stimulant); curare (used by South American hunters to paralyse prey); morphine (poppy juice, for pain and diarrhoea). Such drugs were chosen for their effect, with no idea of a target.

cards.front: What do Indian Ayurveda and Chinese plant-based systems contribute to new medicines, and what does 'ayurveda' mean?
cards.back: They have a strong philosophical and experiential base, and ayurveda also has an experimental basis. 'Ayurveda' means 'science of life' in Sanskrit. The Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas describe the pharmacological and therapeutic properties of more than 700 plants.

cards.front: Which early synthetic substances became drugs before the era of synthetic chemistry, and which is called the first 'rational' therapeutic drug?
cards.back: Diethyl ether and nitrous oxide (Humphry Davy, 1799) were used socially before becoming anaesthetics in the mid-19th century. Amyl nitrite (made 1859) is called the first rational drug, because its benefit in angina was predicted from its physiological actions. Aspirin was first made in 1853 and commercialised by Bayer in 1899.

cards.front: Contrast how plant drugs like atropine or ephedrine came into use with how amyl nitrite did.
cards.back: Plant drugs were adopted from experience of their effects, with no knowledge of any target; use came first and explanation (if any) later. Amyl nitrite worked the other way round: its benefit in angina was predicted from its known physiological actions, which is why it is called the first rational drug.

cards.front: Trace how the way new drugs are found has changed from antiquity to today.
cards.back: Antiquity: remedies from plants chosen by experience, governed by dogma (materia medica). 19th century: purification of active principles (morphine, 1805) showed that chemicals cause drug effects, and synthetic compounds followed (aspirin, amyl nitrite). 20th century: receptor ideas (Langley, Ehrlich) and target-directed drugs (Black's beta-blocker and H2 antagonist). Since the 1980s: biotechnology products and structure-based design. GG14 sums this up as modern drugs being invented, not discovered.

cards.front: Who is regarded as the 'father of pharmacology', and which pupils carried his work forward?
cards.back: Oswald Schmiedeberg (late 19th century). With disciples such as J Langley, T Frazer, P Ehrlich, AJ Clark and JJ Abel he laid down several fundamental concepts of pharmacology.

cards.front: Who founded the first institute of pharmacology, and in which year?
cards.back: Rudolf Buchheim, in 1847, which marked the start of pharmacology as an experimental science. KDT places it in Germany; Rang & Dale say it was set up in his own house in Estonia.

cards.front: Which two physiologists pioneered animal experiments and applied them to the study of drugs?
cards.back: Francois Magendie and his student Claude Bernard (late 18th to 19th century). They developed the methods of experimental physiology and adapted them to study the effects of drugs.

cards.front: Who is called the 'father of Indian pharmacology', and where was India's first pharmacology research centre set up?
cards.back: Sir Ram Nath Chopra. He established the first centre for study and research in pharmacology in India, at the Calcutta School of Tropical Medicine. He held the chair titled Professor of Pharmacology including Indigenous Drugs.

cards.front: Name three pharmacologists from industry who made landmark discoveries, with their contributions.
cards.back: Henry Dale: foundations of chemical transmission and the autonomic nervous system. George Hitchings and Gertrude Elion: the antimetabolite principle and the first effective anticancer drugs. James Black: the first beta-adrenoceptor and histamine H2-receptor antagonists.

cards.front: What is reverse pharmacology, and what did Gananath Sen and Kartik Bose show in 1931?
cards.back: Reverse pharmacology starts from the clinically documented effects of a traditional remedy and then moves to laboratory study, the reverse of the usual laboratory-to-clinic route. Chopra and Sen introduced the concept for Ayurvedic drugs in India. In 1931 Sen and Bose showed that Rauwolfia serpentina had antihypertensive and tranquillising effects.

cards.front: Essay: History of pharmacology

points: Plant remedies from antiquity: opium, belladonna, ma huang, curare
Materia medica guided by dogma; no purification or experimental testing
Magendie and Claude Bernard: animal experiments applied to drugs
Serturner purifies morphine (1805)
Buchheim founds first pharmacology institute (1847)
Schmiedeberg, 'father of pharmacology', and pupils (Langley, Ehrlich, Clark, Abel)
Amyl nitrite (1859) and aspirin (Bayer, 1899)
Ehrlich's receptor idea and arsphenamine for syphilis
Domagk's prontosil (1935); penicillin by Chain and Florey
Langley's receptor concept (1905), developed by Clark, Gaddum, Schild
Discovery of hormones, transmitters, mediators; rise of biochemistry
Sulfanilamide deaths: 1938 safety law
Thalidomide: efficacy and teratogenicity testing (1962)
Receptor purification and cloning from the 1970s; orphan receptors
Biopharmaceuticals since the 1980s; gene and cell therapy
Computer-aided design: drugs now invented rather than discovered

cards.front: Who discovered the first clinically useful sulfonamide, and what did it start?
cards.back: Gerhard Domagk (1935) showed that the dye prontosil was dramatically effective against streptococcal infection. This launched the era of antibacterial chemotherapy, later expanded by penicillin (Fleming's work developed by Chain and Florey during the Second World War).

cards.front: Who first proposed the receptor concept, and who developed it further?
cards.back: Langley proposed receptors for chemical mediators in 1905. The idea was taken up by Clark, Gaddum, Schild and others and remains central to drug discovery and therapeutics.

cards.front: What are biopharmaceuticals, and since when have they become a major source of drugs?
cards.back: Since the 1980s, biotechnology has supplied antibodies, enzymes and regulatory proteins (hormones, growth factors, cytokines), mostly made by genetic engineering. The pharmacological principles are the same as for small molecules, but absorption, distribution, elimination, specificity, toxicity and cost differ greatly. Gene- and cell-based therapies are the next step.

cards.front: How did Paul Ehrlich's work on dyes lead to chemotherapy?
cards.back: Selective staining of tissues by dyes led Ehrlich to propose chemical receptors that 'fixed' the dye, and that microbes might carry unique receptors so a chemical could kill them while sparing host tissue. This produced arsphenamine (salvarsan), an organic arsenical for syphilis (GG14 dates the invention to 1907), used until penicillin arrived.

cards.front: How did receptors change from theoretical entities to molecules that could be studied?
cards.back: In the 1970s receptor-labelling methods allowed receptors to be extracted and purified. Partial amino-acid sequences then allowed cloning; later, expression cloning and genome-based homology cloning identified several hundred receptors. Cloning revealed many subtypes and 'orphan receptors' whose natural ligand is unknown.

cards.front: Why does GG14 argue that modern drugs are 'invented' rather than 'discovered'?
cards.back: Only a fraction of new drugs now come from nature. Most are new compounds optimised against many criteria through repeated cycles of design and experiment (medicinal chemistry, high-throughput screening, structure-based and computer-aided design), so they are created rather than found.

cards.front: Timeline: key US drug laws
cards.text: The Pure Food and Drug Act ({{1906}}) banned mislabelling and adulteration; the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act ({{1938}}) required proof of {{safety}}; the {{Kefauver-Harris}} Amendments (1962) added proof of {{efficacy}}; the {{Orphan Drug}} Amendment (1983) gave incentives for drugs for rare diseases; the 1984 Drug Price Competition Act created abbreviated applications for {{generic}} drugs based on bioequivalence.

cards.front: Which Indian Act regulates the import, manufacture and distribution of drugs, and what does Section 17B empower?
cards.back: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Section 17B empowers government agencies to inspect, seize and confiscate drugs found to be adulterated or spurious.

cards.front: Who must authorise a new drug before it is imported or manufactured in India, including an orphan drug?
cards.back: The CDSCO (Central Drugs Standard Control Organization). Any entity seeking to market a new drug, orphan drugs included, must obtain its authorisation to import or manufacture it.

cards.front: When did India join the WHO drug monitoring programme, and where is its national centre?
cards.back: India joined the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring in 1997. The programme is managed by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre, Sweden. India's national centre is in the Department of Pharmacology, AIIMS, New Delhi.

cards.front: Describe the thalidomide disaster and its regulatory consequence.
cards.back: Thalidomide, launched in Europe in 1957 as a 'non-toxic' sedative and promoted for use in pregnancy, caused phocomelia (seal-like limbs) when taken in the first trimester; about 10,000 children were affected and it was withdrawn worldwide. It led to mandatory teratogenicity testing and, in the USA, the Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 1962. Thalidomide is now used in restricted settings (immunomodulator, leprosy reactions, cancer).

cards.front: Which tragedy prompted the US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act of 1938, and what did the Act require?
cards.back: Deaths from a sulfanilamide preparation marketed before it and its vehicle had been adequately tested. The Act required new drugs to be shown safe as well as pure (proof of efficacy came only in 1962).

cards.front: Link each drug disaster to the law it produced and what that law added.
cards.back: Elixir sulfanilamide deaths led to the 1938 US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act: new drugs must be proved safe. Thalidomide (phocomelia) led to the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments: proof of efficacy as well as safety, and mandatory teratogenicity testing. In India the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (1940) regulates import, manufacture and distribution, with CDSCO authorising new drugs. Pattern: regulation tightens after harm exposes a gap.

cards.front: List the four main protein targets of drugs and give non-protein or unusual targets.
cards.back: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters (carriers). Exceptions: colchicine binds the structural protein tubulin; ciclosporin binds cytosolic immunophilins; some therapeutic antibodies act by sequestering cytokines; antimicrobial and anticancer drugs may target DNA or cell-wall constituents.

cards.front: Give one drug that inhibits an enzyme competitively, one irreversibly, and one acting as a false substrate.
cards.back: Captopril: substrate-analogue competitive inhibitor of angiotensin-converting enzyme. Aspirin: irreversible inhibitor of cyclo-oxygenase. Fluorouracil: replaces uracil in the pathway but cannot be turned into thymidylate, so DNA synthesis and cell division are blocked. Enzymes are one of the four main protein targets.

cards.front: Why are transporters drug targets, and what are ABC transporters?
cards.back: Ions and polar molecules cross membranes through channels or carriers, so blocking a carrier changes how cells handle them (cocaine blocks monoamine uptake into nerve terminals). ABC transporters have an ATP-binding site and use ATP hydrolysis to pump against a gradient: the Na+-K+ ATPase and multidrug-resistance (MDR) transporters that eject cytotoxic drugs and cause resistance. Other carriers couple organic molecules to Na+ by symport or antiport.

cards.front: In what ways can drugs alter ion channel function? Give examples.
cards.back: By binding the agonist (orthosteric) site of a ligand-gated channel; by binding an allosteric site that changes gating (benzodiazepines enhance GABA opening of the GABA-A chloride channel; dihydropyridines inhibit L-type calcium channel opening); or by physically plugging the pore (local anaesthetics in the voltage-gated sodium channel).

cards.front: Why does no drug act with complete specificity, and what are on-target versus off-target side effects?
cards.back: Targets bind classes of drug selectively but not exclusively, so higher doses (or low-potency drugs) reach other targets. On-target effects act through the same receptor as the wanted effect (opioid constipation and respiratory depression); off-target effects arise by a different mechanism (dry mouth from tricyclics, which block other receptors besides monoamine transporters).

cards.front: Compare the four protein target classes: for each give a drug example and say where poor specificity could cause unwanted effects.
cards.back: Receptor: albuterol on beta-2 receptors (the agonist/antagonist distinction applies only here). Enzyme: statins on HMG-CoA reductase, aspirin on COX. Transporter: cocaine or tricyclics on monoamine carriers. Ion channel: local anaesthetics on Na+ channels, benzodiazepines on GABA-A. Specificity is reciprocal but never absolute: tricyclics also hit other receptors, and rising dose widens the targets reached. Exceptions to protein targets include DNA (antimicrobial and antitumour drugs), tubulin (colchicine) and immunophilins (ciclosporin).

cards.front: Classify: the four receptor superfamilies
cards.text: Type 1 {{ligand-gated ion channels}} (ionotropic; e.g. nicotinic, GABA-A; act in {{milliseconds}}); Type 2 {{G protein-coupled receptors}} (metabotropic, 7-transmembrane; e.g. muscarinic, adrenoceptors; seconds); Type 3 {{kinase-linked and related receptors}} (single transmembrane helix; e.g. insulin, growth factor, cytokine receptors); Type 4 {{nuclear receptors}} (regulate {{gene transcription}}; e.g. steroid receptors; hours to days).

cards.front: What are kinase-linked and related receptors, and which non-enzymic receptors belong to this group?
cards.back: Membrane receptors with an extracellular ligand-binding domain joined by one transmembrane helix to an intracellular domain that is often an enzyme (protein kinase or guanylyl cyclase). They respond mainly to protein mediators (insulin, growth factors). Some lack enzyme activity and signal through adaptor proteins, such as cytokine (e.g. TNF) receptors and pattern-recognition receptors of innate immunity.

cards.front: List the four main G protein classes with their effector and a toxin that affects them.
cards.back: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase (cAMP up); cholera toxin keeps it active by blocking its GTPase. Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase (cAMP down); pertussis toxin blocks it. Go acts mainly through beta-gamma subunits and is pertussis-sensitive. Gq activates phospholipase C, giving IP3 and DAG (Ca2+ release, protein kinase C). G12/13 activates Rho and Rho kinase. Different receptors couple to different G proteins, e.g. cardiac M2 and beta-1 receptors give opposite effects.

cards.front: What makes a ligand-gated channel the typical fast receptor, and what is the nicotinic receptor's structure?
cards.back: Type 1 receptors are ionotropic: agonist binding directly opens the pore, giving effects in milliseconds (fast synaptic transmission). The nicotinic ACh receptor is a pentamer of different subunits around a central pore lined by the M2 helices; ACh binding twists the subunits and swivels the kinked M2 segments open. Glutamate receptors (tetramers) and P2X receptors (trimers) have a different architecture.

cards.front: Short note: Nuclear receptors

points: Family of 48 soluble receptors that sense lipid and hormonal signals
Monomeric proteins with N-terminal AF1 domain, DNA-binding core with two zinc fingers, hinge, and C-terminal ligand-binding domain with AF2
Liganded receptor binds hormone response elements (HREs) in gene promoters
Recruits co-activators (e.g. histone acetylases) or co-repressors to change transcription
Endocrine steroid receptors: glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, oestrogen, progesterone, androgen
Cytoplasmic with heat shock proteins; form homodimers and move to nucleus when liganded
Lipid or metabolite ligands: PPAR, LXR, FXR, PXR/SXR, CAR
Mostly nuclear; heterodimers with retinoid X receptor (RXR)
PXR and CAR induce drug-metabolising enzymes such as CYP3A
Target of about 10% of prescription drugs
Enzymes they control affect the kinetics of about 60% of prescription drugs
Selective modulators (e.g. SERMs) act as agonist in some tissues, antagonist in others

cards.front: Short note: Present status of purinergic receptors

points: Adenosine (P1) receptors A1, A2A, A2B and A3: G protein-coupled, act on cAMP
P2Y receptors (P2Y1 to P2Y14): G protein-coupled, some respond to pyrimidines
P2X receptors (P2X1 to P2X7): trimeric ATP-gated cation channels
ATP acts mainly on P2X receptors; ADP acts mainly on P2Y receptors
ADP released from platelets promotes aggregation through P2Y12
ATP is released from damaged cells and acts as a neurotransmitter
Clopidogrel and prasugrel (prodrugs), ticagrelor and cangrelor block platelet P2Y12
Used with aspirin to prevent arterial thromboembolic disorders
Caffeine and theophylline block adenosine receptors
Regadenoson, a selective A2A agonist, is used as a cardiac diagnostic vasodilator
Suramin blocks many P2X and P2Y receptors but is non-selective
More selective ATP antagonists are still in development
Purinergic drugs are being explored for pain, thrombosis and inflammation

cards.front: Describe the G protein activation cycle and why the signal is self-limiting.
cards.back: Agonist-bound receptor makes the alpha subunit swap GDP for GTP; alpha-GTP leaves the receptor and the beta-gamma complex and acts on an effector. The alpha subunit's own GTPase hydrolyses GTP to GDP, ending the signal; alpha-GDP rejoins beta-gamma. Binding of the effector speeds the GTPase, so effector activation limits itself. Cholera toxin blocks the GTPase, so Gs stays active.

cards.front: Essay: Molecular basis of drug action

points: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters
Exceptions: tubulin (colchicine), immunophilins (ciclosporin), DNA
Ligand-gated ion channels (ms)
GPCRs (s), largest family
Kinase-linked receptors (protein mediators)
Nuclear receptors (h to days), class I steroid and class II RXR heterodimers
Selectivity and gating
Block of pore (local anaesthetics), allosteric modulation (benzodiazepines, dihydropyridines)
Two-state model
Constitutive activity and inverse agonism
Biased agonism
Desensitisation: GRK phosphorylation, internalisation
Dimerisation and RAMPs
Arrestin signalling
Receptor labelling, purification and cloning
Expression in cell lines; crystallography; orphan receptors

cards.front: What is biased agonism?
cards.back: Different agonists acting at the same site on one receptor favour different downstream pathways, because they stabilise different active (R*) states. Examples include ligands at angiotensin receptors and inverse agonists at beta-adrenoceptors. It adds a dimension to efficacy beyond affinity and intrinsic activity.

cards.front: What are receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMPs)? Give the classic example.
cards.back: Membrane proteins that associate with some GPCRs (mostly class B peptide receptors) and change their pharmacology. Calcitonin receptor-like receptor is inactive alone; with RAMP1 it becomes the CGRP receptor, and with RAMP2 it becomes an adrenomedullin receptor.

cards.front: How are G protein-coupled receptors desensitised?
cards.back: Two main processes: phosphorylation of serine and threonine residues (mainly in the C-terminal tail) by GPCR kinases (GRKs) or by PKA and PKC, and internalisation (endocytosis) of the receptor. Homologous desensitisation affects only the receptor activated by the agonist; heterologous desensitisation also affects other GPCRs.

cards.front: What is constitutive receptor activity, and how does an inverse agonist differ from a neutral antagonist?
cards.back: Some receptors (e.g. benzodiazepine, cannabinoid and serotonin receptors; histamine H3 even in vivo) show activation with no ligand bound, also caused by some disease mutations. An inverse agonist lowers this basal activity (negative efficacy); a neutral antagonist only blocks agonists. Most clinical antagonists behave as inverse agonists in constitutively active systems.

cards.front: Explain the two-state model of receptor activation.
cards.back: The receptor switches between a resting state (R) and an active state (R*), which may exist even without ligand. A ligand with higher affinity for R* shifts the balance towards activation (agonist; full or partial depending on the size of the preference); one with equal affinity is a neutral antagonist; one preferring R is an inverse agonist. Its weakness is that receptors actually adopt many conformations.

cards.front: Short note: Newer concepts in GPCR biology

points: One gene, one receptor protein, one G protein, one response
GABA-B functions only as a heterodimer of two subunits
Most GPCRs can form homo- or hetero-oligomers, e.g. opioid receptor heterodimers, dopamine D2 with somatostatin receptors
Dopamine D5 can directly inhibit the GABA-A channel
RAMPs change agonist specificity (CRLR with RAMP1 = CGRP receptor)
Constitutive activity: inverse agonists differ from neutral antagonists
Biased agonism: different agonists select different pathways
Arrestins bound to the receptor can activate the MAP kinase cascade
Cross-talk with tyrosine-kinase adaptor proteins

cards.front: How are ion channels characterised, and what are the main gating types?
cards.back: By ion selectivity (set by pore size and lining; cation or anion selective) and by gating. Gating types: voltage-gated (open on depolarisation, then inactivate; Na+, K+, Ca2+ channels), ligand-gated by extracellular transmitters (glutamate, ACh, GABA, 5-HT, ATP), channels gated by intracellular signals (Ca2+-activated K+ and Cl- channels, ATP-sensitive K+ channels), calcium-release channels (IP3 and ryanodine receptors) and store-operated channels.

cards.front: Give an example of a ligand-gated channel that responds to the local environment rather than a transmitter.
cards.back: TRPV1 on sensory nerves: activated by capsaicin, by protons when tissue pH falls in inflammation, and by heat.

cards.front: Name the three ways drugs can change ion channel function, with an example of each.
cards.back: 1) Direct binding to the channel: orthosteric site, allosteric site (benzodiazepines, dihydropyridines) or pore plug (local anaesthetics). 2) Indirect, through a G protein subunit or other intermediary. 3) Altering channel expression at the cell surface (gabapentin reduces insertion of neuronal calcium channels).

cards.front: Where are IP3 receptors and ryanodine receptors, and why are they called ligand-gated channels?
cards.back: They sit on the endoplasmic or sarcoplasmic reticulum, not the plasma membrane. They are a special class of ligand-gated calcium channel, opened by intracellular signals, that release Ca2+ from intracellular stores into the cytosol. Store-operated channels in the plasma membrane open when those stores are depleted.

cards.front: Name the sites where drugs act on the voltage-gated sodium channel, with examples.
cards.back: Channel block: tetrodotoxin and saxitoxin, plus local anaesthetics, antiepileptics (phenytoin) and antidysrhythmics. Block of inactivation (channel stays open): veratridine, batrachotoxin, scorpion toxins, DDT and pyrethroids. Gating is also altered by phosphorylation by PKA or PKC after GPCR activation. Multiple binding sites are typical of many ion channels.

cards.front: Distinguish a pore blocker, an allosteric modulator and an expression modulator of ion channels.
cards.back: Pore blocker (local anaesthetics on the Na+ channel) physically plugs the channel. Allosteric modulator binds a separate site and changes gating: benzodiazepines facilitate GABA-triggered opening of the GABA-A Cl- channel (so they work with GABA), dihydropyridines inhibit opening of L-type Ca2+ channels. Expression modulator (gabapentin) reduces the number of channels inserted in the membrane.

cards.front: Tabulate ion channels as drug targets with examples.
cards.back: Ligand-gated (extracellular ligand): nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, glutamate, 5-HT3, P2X; benzodiazepines act on GABA-A. Voltage-gated: Na+ (local anaesthetics, phenytoin), Ca2+ (dihydropyridines; gabapentin reduces insertion), K+ (more than 70 subtypes). Gated by intracellular signals: Ca2+-activated K+ and Cl- channels; ATP-sensitive K+ channel (partner of the sulfonylurea receptor, closed by ATP). Intracellular Ca2+ release channels: IP3 and ryanodine receptors. Store-operated Ca2+ channels. Environment-sensitive: TRPV1 (capsaicin, protons, heat). Drug mechanisms: pore block, allosteric gating change, indirect modulation, altered expression.

cards.front: Distinguish affinity from efficacy, and say what each tells you about an agonist, a partial agonist and a simple antagonist.
cards.back: Affinity is the tendency to bind the receptor (occupation); efficacy is the ability, once bound, to activate it. An agonist has both. A partial agonist binds but activates less, so it cannot give the full response. A simple antagonist has affinity but zero efficacy, so it only blocks agonists. This split is why binding alone never predicts a drug's effect.

cards.front: Essay: Central excitatory neurotransmitters

points: Glutamate and aspartate are the main excitatory amino acid transmitters in the brain
Glutamate is the most abundant and the principal fast excitatory transmitter
NMDA, AMPA and kainate receptors are ligand-gated ion channels
NMDA receptors need glutamate plus a co-agonist (glycine) to open
NMDA receptors are Ca2+ permeable
Metabotropic glutamate receptors are GPCRs (mGluRs)
Fast synaptic excitation
Long-term potentiation and long-term depression, the proposed basis of learning and memory
Neuronal and glial transporters remove glutamate from the synapse
Glial EAAT1 and EAAT2 carry most of the uptake and limit excitotoxicity
Excess glutamate causes excitotoxicity in stroke, ischaemia and neurodegeneration
Memantine blocks NMDA receptors in a use-dependent way
Antiseizure drugs such as valproate and phenytoin reduce glutamate release or block NMDA responses
GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter, acting through Cl- channels (GABAA) or GPCRs (GABAB)

cards.front: What is the NMDA receptor, and what two agonists does it need?
cards.back: An ionotropic glutamate receptor (ligand-gated Ca2+-permeable cation channel). It needs glutamate plus glycine to open.

cards.front: What are EAAT1 and EAAT2, and why do they matter?
cards.back: Glial glutamate transporters that take up most of the synaptic glutamate; they limit excitotoxic damage.

cards.front: Essay: Drug discovery techniques

points: Early drugs were found by serendipity; modern discovery starts from a chosen target
Drug discovery in the past often came from observing effects of plant extracts or chemicals
Plants: morphine, ephedrine, quinine, curare, atropine, artemisinin
Animal products: adrenaline, thyroxine, insulin, liver extract
Microbes: penicillin (1941) opened the antibiotic source
Natural products mostly serve as lead compounds
Random synthesis has low chance of a useful hit; now rarely used (barbiturates and chlorpromazine were serendipitous)
Chemical congeners of natural products are made to improve properties
Validated target leads to a clinical candidate, refined by structure-activity relationships
High-throughput screening of chemical libraries on cells, enzymes or receptors (phenotypic or target-based)
Combinatorial chemistry generates many compounds for robotic screening; failure rates are high
Three-dimensional protein structures allow molecular modelling and docking
Selective COX-2 inhibitors were designed from differences between COX-1 and COX-2
Recombinant proteins (insulin, growth hormone, interferon), monoclonal antibodies
Pharmacogenomics aims at individualised drugs

cards.front: What is a lead compound?
cards.back: A compound (often natural) with a useful activity that is chemically modified to give a better drug.

cards.front: What is combinatorial chemistry?
cards.back: Combining chemical groups in many ways to make large numbers of compounds, which are then screened in automated assays.

cards.front: Essay: Tools and techniques to study ion channels

points: Ion channels are membrane proteins that form ion-selective pores; many drugs act on them
Study methods range from current recording to structure and molecular genetics
Voltage clamp: holds membrane potential and records macroscopic currents; used since the 1950s (squid axon work)
Pharmacological separation of Na+ and K+ currents with blockers such as TTX and TEA
Devised by Neher and Sakmann; measures current through a single channel
Showed a physical pore (about 10^7 ions/s) and that conductance is the same for all agonists while open time varies
Gives gating kinetics and permeability of ligand-gated and voltage-gated channels
Radioligand binding measures receptor occupancy and density (Bmax)
Torpedo nicotinic receptor purified and characterised as a pentamer (four subunit types)
X-ray crystallography and NMR give three-dimensional structures; docking models ligand binding
Cloning and expression cloning; recombinant expression systems
Site-directed mutagenesis maps residues that form binding sites or gates
Combine recording, binding, structure and mutagenesis to link a drug's site to its effect on channel gating

cards.front: What does the patch clamp technique measure?
cards.back: The very small current passing through a single ion channel; devised by Neher and Sakmann.

cards.front: What does voltage clamp measure, and what did it first reveal?
cards.back: Membrane current at a fixed voltage; Hodgkin and Huxley used it on the squid giant axon to show sodium and potassium currents.

cards.front: Essay: Endoplasmic reticulum and calcium dynamics in neurodegenerative disease

points: Cytosolic Ca2+ is a second messenger, kept low by pumps in the plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
Gq activates phospholipase C; IP3 is made and mobilises Ca2+ from ER stores
IP3 receptors and ryanodine receptors are intracellular ligand-gated Ca2+ release channels
SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum; phospholamban inhibits it when not phosphorylated
RyR1 in skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum
Abnormal ryanodine receptor underlies malignant hyperthermia triggered by halothane
Excess glutamate overactivates NMDA receptors, causing Ca2+ overload and neuronal death
Free radicals and toxins such as MPTP add to damage in Parkinson's disease
Loss of 70-80% of dopamine neurons at symptomatic stage; Lewy bodies made of aggregated alpha-synuclein
Memantine reduces excitotoxicity by use-dependent NMDA blockade
Neuroprotection targets excitotoxicity; the books reviewed do not show a drug acting on ER calcium stores in these diseases

cards.front: What is excitotoxicity?
cards.back: Neuronal injury caused by excess glutamate, mainly through NMDA-receptor Ca2+ overload.

cards.front: What is the ryanodine receptor?
cards.back: An intracellular Ca2+ release channel on the sarcoplasmic reticulum; abnormal in malignant hyperthermia.

cards.front: What is SERCA?
cards.back: Sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase; pumps cytosolic Ca2+ back into the store. Phospholamban inhibits it.
